body.text: The EU Generalized Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+) was launched to provide exemptions to vulnerable and developing countries. The scheme was special because it lifted tariffs on almost two-thirds of EU tariff lines. For an economy like Pakistan’s, it has been a lifeline in building exports and filling up its coffers. GSP+ is also designed to incentivise commitments on international human rights, labor laws, environmental safeguards, and governance improvements, so participation would benefit Pakistan in non-economic ways as well. Pakistan joined the scheme in 2014 and has been its biggest beneficiary.

GSP+ really boomed trade, especially Pakistani exports to the EU. In 2025 alone, bilateral trade totalled 12.2 billion euro, with Pakistan enjoying a 5.2 billion euro trade surplus. According to the latest figures published for 2024, a total of 7.5 billion euros’ worth of exports were eligible for the scheme, which generated an estimated 732 million euros in tariff exemptions for Pakistan, making Pakistani exports more competitive and attractive.

However, there is a caveat. Although Pakistan’s exports are high, they have yet to reach their 2022 peak – 9.50 billion euro in 2022 vs 8.68 billion euro in 2025 – signalling an underlying problem. Textiles and textile articles accounted for 77.7 percent of Pakistan’s exports to the EU in 2025, concentrating exports and posing a risk, according to the EU Commission’s own Trade and Economic Security profile on Pakistan.

India is close to a similar tariff-access agreement with the EU, and Pakistan has to adhere to a stricter set of international conventions to maintain its GSP+ status in the next cycle. The problem is no longer being part of the GSP+, but how Pakistan can use this benefit to become more diversified and competitive before this access loses its edge.
A Surplus That Hides a Plateau

Pakistan has come a long way since 2014, with exports rising from 4.29 billion euro in 2014 to 8.68 billion euro in 2025. But not everything is going smoothly on that ascent. In 2022, Pakistan achieved its highest export value to the EU, totaling 9.50 billion euro, which then dropped significantly to 7.97 billion euro in 2023 before rising to 8.68 billion euro by 2025. The decline in 2023 can be attributed to a number of factors, including the post-COVID shock, low demand for textiles in Europe, and Pakistan’s own economic problems, including record-high inflation, devaluation of the rupee, import restrictions, and floods that hit the country and disrupted industrial production and exports.

Even though, as previously mentioned, Pakistani exports haven’t returned to their 2022 peak, Pakistan’s trade surplus with the EU has risen from 4.12 billion euro in 2022 to 5.17 billion euro in 2025. This was due to Pakistan’s imports from the EU dropping from 5.39 billion euro in 2022 to 3.52 billion euro in 2025. Therefore, Pakistan’s record surplus should not necessarily be lauded or attributed to its competitiveness; it’s just the simple math of decreasing imports into Pakistan from the EU.

Nor is the issue whether or not the exporters are taking advantage of the preferences they have available to them. “GSP+-eligible” imports relate to goods falling within tariff lines eligible for the preferential treatment of the scheme. At the same time, the utilization rate refers to the share of eligible imports that enter the EU under the GSP+ scheme. In 2024, 90.4 percent of EU imports from Pakistan qualified for the GSP+ provisions, while Pakistani exporters benefited from 95.1 percent of the preferences. The mechanism is doing exactly what it was designed to do.

The problem is the use to which it is being put. Textiles and textile articles alone contributed 77.7 percent of EU imports from Pakistan in 2025. The next-biggest sectors were raw hides at 4 percent, vegetable products at 3.7 percent, foodstuffs and beverages at 3.1 percent, and miscellaneous manufactured goods at 2.6 percent. The preferential treatment for exports has thus been in place for over a decade or more and has increased exports without significantly altering their composition. A failure of this sort does not mean GSP+ was a failure. It is the successful use of preferential access by Pakistan, but not the use of that opportunity to diversify to an adequate extent.
India Changes the Competitive Equation

The second pressure comes from next door. In January 2026, India and the EU concluded negotiations on a long-awaited free trade agreement. As South Asian Voices has noted, the deal may affect the economic landscape of South Asia. In Pakistan, one immediate implication will be that the advantage its exporters have had in Europe will lose its distinctiveness.

According to the agreed deal, duty-free access will be granted to Indian apparel and textiles, which were previously subject to duties of up to 12 percent. The agreement must undergo legal processes before its provisions take effect, and it doesn’t necessarily mean that Indian companies will replace Pakistani exporters. Pakistan continues to have loyal European customers and commanding stakes in cotton garments and home textiles. However, the competitive balance changes once a large regional competitor no longer faces a tariff disadvantage.

Pakistan can’t match the magnitude of India by merely attempting to export more of the same low-value textile products. Competing differently means additional diversification into more specialized and more valuable products, faster delivery times, higher productivity and energy reliability, and more traceability and standards compliance, something that European buyers are increasingly demanding.

The opportunity also extends beyond textiles. Pakistan Business Council research identifies optical, medical, and surgical instruments as “rising stars,” while pharmaceuticals and machinery appear among the “lost opportunities” where EU demand has grown faster than Pakistan’s exports. The gap is also striking in medical and surgical instruments, where the EU imported approximately $24.9 billion globally in 2024, while Pakistan supplied only $128.7 million despite exporting $446.6 million in the same category worldwide. Other avenues of expanding the export base include processed foods, engineering and electrical products, and higher value finished goods. The message isn’t to give up on textiles; it’s to end the practice of trying to shoulder almost all of the burden for the European relationship with one industry.
The Next GSP+ Test Goes Beyond Renewal

Pakistan also has a near-term policy challenge. The EU will be rolling out new GSP regulations as of January 1, 2027. Current beneficiaries of GSP+ will be given their preferences over a two-year transition period until the end of 2028, but will need to re-apply for GSP+ following the new admission criteria. The framework increases the number of related international conventions from 27 to 32, and current beneficiaries will be required to ratify six new conventions and provide a plan to implement the full set of conventions going forward. It also enhances monitoring and enables the quicker withdrawal of preferences in cases of serious violations.

That is significant because the EU 2026 Pakistan report noted Pakistan’s progress in areas such as labor rights legislation and anti-torture laws, but also reported that it had “regressed in several areas, while positive change was limited” and that enforcement was a recurring weakness. Reapplication should not, therefore, be a diplomatic exercise out of the context of domestic implementation.

The commercial rules are changing too as the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism has gone into effect, though textiles are not currently covered under this regime. The more immediate challenge for Pakistani exporters is the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation and the coming Digital Product Passport (DPP). The passport is effectively a digital record that contains product information on composition, origin, sustainability, traceability, and compliance. Textile apparel is a priority product group, with the European Commission planning textile-specific rules for late 2027. Following adoption, businesses will have a transition period of at least 18 months before the requirements become applicable.

For Pakistan, this is not an abstract environmental requirement, as even with tariffs at zero, firms lacking a reliable supply chain and product information might be less able to retain European buyers. Islamabad should therefore now engage with textile and apparel associations, chambers of commerce, exporters, certification bodies, and standardization experts to create a common system of traceability and reporting, rather than burdening individual companies, particularly small ones, with the task of interpreting new EU requirements.
From Access to Competitiveness

Going forward, Pakistan should focus on three priorities. Firstly, Islamabad should regard the re-application for GSP+ as a whole-of-government compliance program and rectify shortcomings in EU monitoring well before the stipulated deadline at the end of 2028. Secondly, export policy should focus on strengthening the sectors where Pakistan has production capacity but is limited in the European market, such as medical and surgical instruments, pharmaceuticals, processed foods, engineering and electrical goods, and high-value textile products. Thirdly, government and industry should prepare exporters for Europe’s new traceability and sustainability requirements before they become costly barriers to market access.

GSP+ has provided Pakistan with unparalleled access to one of the world’s largest markets for the past 12 years. That access remains valuable; however, the idea of preferential access was never meant to replace competitiveness. In a nutshell, Pakistan’s EU trade boom is not simply ending, nor is GSP+ the problem. The more difficult reality is that preferential access has taken Pakistan about as far as it can without deeper reforms at home. With the beginning of India’s access to the same market and the evolving regulatory model in Europe, that weakness is being revealed. Preserving GSP+ is important, but it is more important to convert preference into competitiveness.
